bib.title: Eliciting Human Preferences with Language Models

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Eliciting Human Preferences with Language Models", Belinda Z. Li, Alex Tamkin, Noah Goodman, Jacob Andreas (MIT CSAIL, Anthropic, Stanford). arXiv:2310.11589v1 [cs.CL], 17 Oct 2023. The PDF header shows only the arXiv preprint. It carries no venue line, so I cannot confirm a later venue from it.
COVERAGE: all 26 pages, about 78.7k chars read. I read main text, references (skimmed), appendices A to F and the limitations. Appendix A holds the prompts (extraction lines 738-818). I skimmed it and it holds no results. No extraction fault. The results are bar charts (Figs 3, 4, 9-15), so the text gives NO numeric effect sizes, confidence intervals or p-values for the main comparison.

NOTE CHECK. The note line 135 reads: "GATE has language models elicit a user's intent through open-ended questions and edge cases; in preregistered experiments across three domains, users reported less effort than writing prompts or labelling examples, and the process surfaced considerations they had not anticipated". Two findings from the paper are missing from the note, and one wording is looser than the paper:
- The note leaves out the accuracy and informativeness result.
- It leaves out the fact that significance was shown only in two of three domains.
- "Less effort than ... labelling examples" overreaches. The paper compares effort with user-written prompts. In Fig 4 text, GATE is "equally or less mentally demanding than user-written prompts". Labelling-based methods (supervised learning, active learning) were themselves rated the least demanding (see the Fig 4 claim below).
- "Open-ended questions" were not the lowest-effort GATE method. Labelling and yes/no were.
- Verify "surfaced considerations" against Fig 14. The text gives no numbers.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- claim: Preregistered human studies in 3 domains with GPT-4 as elicitor and predictor; GATE elicits preferences that predict held-out user labels better than no elicitation.
  number: significant at 0.05 in all domains except email, where only generative active learning was significant
  setup: Metric is area under the Δp(correct)-vs-time curve over a 5-minute elicitation. GPT-4 gpt-4-0613, temperature 0.
  quote: "GATE improves over no elicitation ... This is the case across all domains studied (a positive score in Figure 3), with significance at the 0.05 level for all but the email domain, where only generative active learning was significant."
  where: p7, Section 5
- claim: GATE beats user-written prompts in most settings; yes/no questions beat prompts in every setting.
  number: 6/10 settings (absolute), 7/10 (AUC)
  setup: Settings are domain x GATE-method pairs. The moral domain was underpowered.
  quote: "In the majority of settings (6/10 for absolute, 7/10 for AUC), GATE elicitation methods improve over user-written prompts. In particular, generative yes/no questions improve over user-written prompts in every setting studied (although we lack enough power to assess significance in the moral reasoning domain)."
  where: p7
- claim: In content recommendation, GATE (especially open-ended questions) significantly beats supervised learning and pool-based active learning. The Fig 3 caption says significance between GATE and baselines was established only in content recommendation and email.
  number: none
  setup: Supervised and pool-based baselines were run only in content recommendation. Pool is the Microsoft News Dataset (MIND), 160k articles, diversity sampling over 15 clusters.
  quote: "in the content recommendation setting, GATE elicitation methods (particularly generative open-ended questions) significantly improve over supervised learning and pool-based active learning."
  where: p7-8
- claim: Perceived mental effort was equal or lower for interactive methods than for writing a prompt, especially labelling and yes/no.
  number: Likert 1 (Very Little) to 7 (Very High); the text reports no mean ratings
  setup: Question was "How mentally demanding was interacting with the chatbot?" (prompting: "writing your answer"), wording from NASA TLX. Plotted in Fig 4 left.
  quote: "users generally find interactive elicitation methods to be less mentally demanding, especially ones that involve labeling samples or answering yes/no questions, than non-interactive prompting."
  where: p8; method p7
- claim: Users overestimate how well their prompts cover their preferences.
  number: content recommendation 5.3 to 3.9; moral 5.4 to 4.8
  setup: Perceived coverage on a 1-7 Likert scale, rated before and after seeing the test cases, for the prompting condition (the text does not state the condition explicitly; Fig 13 shows each method).
  quote: "reflected in the average rating of their perceived coverage dropping from an average of 5.3 to 3.9 (in the content recommendation domain) and an average of 5.4 to 4.8 (in the moral reasoning domain) after seeing the test cases."
  where: p25, Appendix E.2
- claim: GATE surfaces considerations users had not thought of, more in the moral and email domains than in content recommendation.
  number: none (Fig 14, Likert)
  setup: Question 2: "To what extent did the chatbot raise issues or aspects about your preferences that you hadn't previously considered?"
  quote: "the generative elicitation methods were on average able to surface more novel considerations in the moral reasoning and email validation domains than in the content recommendation domain"
  where: p26
- claim: User-written prompts slightly hurt prediction in the email domain, because users misstate their own rules.
  number: none
  setup: Email domain. Example: a user wrote "an email address should finish with .com or co.uk" but later accepted user@domain.edu. The authors say it may be noise.
  quote: "user-written preferences slightly decrease performance relative to a no-elicitation baseline."
  where: p9
- claim: LM elicitation did not shift users' own preferences.
  number: none (Fig 4 right scatter near y=x)
  quote: "we see no such effect."
  where: p8
- claim: Preferences vary enough across people for elicitation to matter.
  number: 0.77 bits
  setup: Average entropy of p(yes) per question across participants.
  quote: "for an average entropy of 0.77 bits."
  where: p8
- claim: LM-simulated personas predict human results in content and email, not moral.
  number: none
  setup: Model-model runs use 5 turns as the effort proxy. Fig 12.
  quote: "We found that model could simulate humans well in the content recommendation and email validation domains, but not in the moral reasoning domain."
  where: p9, Appendix D

SETUP DETAILS
- Domains and test sets:
  - Content recommendation: predict whether the user would read held-out online articles. The authors collected the test cases.
  - Moral reasoning: when, if ever, is it ethical to steal a loaf of bread. Authors wrote the test scenarios.
  - Email validation: requirements for email address validity. Authors wrote the test emails. Participants were also recruited from US CS programs.
- Procedure: each user interacts with an elicitation policy for 5 minutes, then labels held-out examples. The model predicts a probability of "yes" from the transcript.
- Participants: 388 total. Quote: "We recruited 20–30 participants for each domain-method pair (6 elicitation methods across 3 domains), for a total of 388 participants. Participants were paid an average of $12/hr."
- Recruitment: Prolific, English-speaking. IRB approved. Preregistration at https://osf.io/5v6nd/.
- Table B.1 (rows are conditions; columns are Content / Moral / Email / Total):
  - Supervised learning: 30 / - / - / 30
  - Pool-based active learning: 31 / - / - / 31
  - Prompting: 30 / 30 / 26 / 86
  - Generative active learning: 30 / 30 / 20 / 80
  - Generative yes/no: 31 / 30 / 19 / 80
  - Generative open-ended: 31 / 31 / 19 / 81
  - Total: 183 / 121 / 84 / 388
- Conditions are six: supervised, pool-based active learning, user-written prompt, and three GATE variants (generative active learning = LM-generated edge cases to label, yes/no questions, open-ended questions).
- Metrics:
  - p(correct), the probability the model assigns to the user's answer.
  - Area under the Δp(correct)-vs-time curve (speed of information gain).
  - AUROC variant in the appendix: same trends but smaller Δ and higher variance, so harder to show significance.
  - Perceived effort (Likert 1-7).
  - Usability questions in Appendix E.

LIMITS
- The authors concede (Appendix F) that significance was not established in certain domains due to budget, and the sample is English-speaking and US-based. The moral domain is "very simplistic". Work is limited to prompt-based approaches, with no explicit optimization of the objective in Eq. 2.
- Quote: "we did not have the budget to survey a massive number of humans for human experiments. Thus, we were unable to establish statistical significance of GATE above baselines in certain domains."
- Only GPT-4 (gpt-4-0613, closed and being deprecated). Test cases were author-built. No real deployed task. Users may not have followed the instruction to ignore the transcript when it conflicted with their intuition.
- Dated: 2023, GPT-4 only.
- Phrases that hedge the claim: "often more informative", "(sometimes) more accurately", "initial evidence".
- Ethics: privacy via thin slicing and automation bias.
- Calibration issue: binary yes/no prediction pilots gave skewed all-yes or all-no output, so they used probability-in-token-space.

BUILDS ON: active learning (Cohn et al. 1994; Lewis & Gale 1994; Settles 2009); Tamkin et al. 2022a (task ambiguity) and 2022b (active learning for the intended task); Margatina et al. 2023 (active learning for in-context learning, diversity sampling); Brown et al. 2020 (prompting); Sentence-BERT (Reimers & Gurevych 2019); MIND dataset (Wu et al. 2020); NASA-TLX (Hart & Staveland 1988); requirements elicitation literature and protocol analysis (Ericsson & Simon 1980).

CODE: none in the paper. Code is at https://github.com/alextamkin/generative-elicitation. Prompts are in Appendix A (p16-17). Elicitation prompt style: "Your task is to [learn what topics a user is interested in reading online article about ... go for breadth rather than depth ...]".

FIGURES (captions in extraction only; charts are images):
- Fig 1, p2: the three-panel schematic comparing prompting, active learning and generative elicitation. It is the quickest explanation of the method.
- Fig 2, p4: 2x2 grid of passive vs interactive and example-based vs free-form.
- Fig 3, p8: AUC of Δp(correct) vs time per method and domain. This is the main result chart.
- Fig 4, p9: left, perceived mental demand; right, scatter showing no preference shift.
- Fig 5, p10: sample transcripts per domain and method.
- Fig 13, 14, 15, p25-26: perceived coverage, novelty and transcript reuse.
- Fig 9, p21: AUROC variant.
- Figs 10-12, p23-24: model-model simulation results.

PROBLEMS: No embedded instructions found. The text extraction gives no table of effect sizes, so any numeric effect (for example the size of the gain over prompts) cannot be quoted. It would have to be read off Fig 3 and Fig 4 as images. A figure caption command was not run. Appendix A prompts were skimmed, not read line by line.
